night.Japanese_action: Fragmented but deliberate local cells conduct four to six infiltration/local counterattack actions rather than one mass charge. Roughly 260-380 men participate over the night, with the largest packet around 70-110. Targets are artillery/observer positions, road junctions, tank harbors, beach-exit traffic and local command posts.
night.local_success: At one or two points Japanese groups penetrate roughly 100-180 m and briefly interrupt a road/support lane for 20-45 minutes. No cross-island breakthrough and no beachhead-ejection attack forms because command and communications cannot synchronize the remaining defense.
night.US_response: Tarawa-informed final protective fires, star shells, battalion mortars/artillery, tanks held as mobile stop-lines and destroyer illumination/direct fire. Dense night traffic and close friendly lines force short pauses and produce some normal friendly-fire/accident friction.
night.dawn_state: About 1,650-2,050 organized/local fighters plus 420-600 scattered/support personnel remain capable of local defense.

daylight_7Feb.US_method: Advance is deliberately paced around engineer-cleared lanes and observed strongpoints: suppress, tank/direct-fire approach, engineer/flamethrower/demolition action where needed, infantry occupation, then recheck for remanned positions. Later waves and heavy equipment are metered through improved beach exits rather than simply added to the queue.
daylight_7Feb.advance: Strong axes gain another roughly 0.8-1.1 km. By T24 the US controls or dominates about 65-75 percent of Kwajalein Island, including most of the western/airfield zone; the northeastern cantonment/defense belt remains contested.
daylight_7Feb.vehicles: D-Day temporary LVT mission-kills partly recover; roughly 7-10 of the short-repair vehicles return during D+1. Additional medium tanks and engineer equipment come ashore, but road/debris clearance remains the pacing constraint rather than raw tank count.

Japan_T24.command: No island-wide counterattack capability. Several mutually supporting local strongpoint clusters still exist in the northeast.

assessment: Kwajalein remains the main resistance problem. Better pre-registered fires, shelters, ammunition distribution and local communications buy another costly day, but US tanks/engineers/direct fire and improving beach logistics steadily convert material superiority into ground.
